svg.aria-label: The independence assumption stated, measured as a lift ratio, and shown to be false by a factor of about 1.9 on the planted token clusters
svg.text: THE ASSUMPTION, AND HOW FALSE IT IS
Everyone says the independence assumption is wrong. Almost nobody measures it. One ratio does.
What Naive Bayes believes about every pair of tokens, given the class:
P(a, b | class) == P(a | class) x P(b | class)
Divide one side by the other and you get a lift.
If the assumption holds, lift is 1.00. Nothing else to know.
WHAT THE INBOX ACTUALLY SHOWS
the planted clusters, measured (lift, 1.00 = assumption holds)
login_access otp + 2fa
billing card + charged
bug_crash error + exception
shipping delivery + tracking
Those pairs co-occur nearly twice as often as the model can represent.
The assumption is not approximately true here. It is plainly false.
AND IT IS FINDABLE WITHOUT AN ANSWER KEY
The same ratio, swept blindly across every token pair with no
answer key, ranked by distance from 1.00:
top 27 flags 14 genuine 52% precision 52% recall
top 60 flags 25 genuine 42% precision 93% recall
top 100 flags 27 genuine 27% precision 100% recall
Widen the list and recall rises while precision falls. That is the
same trade you face on real tickets, where nothing tells you which
flags were real and the 3% class throws false positives on noise.
SO WHY MEASURE A RATIO AND NOT RUN A TEST?
A chi-square on these pairs returns p-values below 1e-40. It also returns p < 0.001 for pairs whose lift is 1.02,
because at 9,000 tickets significance is cheap. The p-value tells you the violation is real; only the effect size
tells you whether it matters. Both columns are in the output, side by side, for exactly that reason.
